conventions.convention: A real field requires coordinate measurability on one common probability space. Joint measurability is an additional hypothesis for spatial integration.

Strict stationarity means invariance of finite-dimensional laws under every common translation that keeps the listed sites in T. Wide stationarity requires square-integrable coordinates, constant mean, and Cov(X(s),X(t)) = C(t-s).

Order-two intrinsic stationarity requires finite increment first and second raw moments depending only on displacement. The variogram is half the increment second raw moment; increment means need not vanish and level second moments need not exist. This convention agrees with Spodarev 2024, §§1.1–1.2: https://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/website_uni_ulm/mawi.inst.110/lehre/ss24/SpatialStatistics_2024.pdf.
The CND theorem is stated for fields indexed by all of ℝᵈ and tests real coefficients whose sum is zero. Its proof is choice-free.

Gaussian existence assumes AC, permits singular finite covariance matrices, and gives a unique law only on the cylinder sigma-algebra. It asserts neither sample-path continuity nor joint measurability and includes the empty index set.

The spatial Bochner theorem assumes AC and DC and continuity of the covariance on ℝᵈ. Its representation uses the positive character phase on the Pontryagin dual and asserts a finite positive Radon measure, with no density conclusion.

load_bearing.statement: A real random field is a family of coordinate-measurable real random variables on one probability space. Wide stationarity requires square-integrable coordinates, constant mean, and covariance C(t-s). Order-two intrinsic stationarity requires displacement-only finite increment first and second raw moments, with γ(h) = ½E[(X(s+h)-X(s))²].
For a real random field on one probability space with every coordinate square-integrable, K(s,t) = Cov(X(s),X(t)) is symmetric and every finite real quadratic form ΣᵢⱼaᵢaⱼK(sᵢ,sⱼ) is nonnegative.

For an order-two intrinsically stationary real field on ℝᵈ, every finite real zero-sum coefficient family satisfies Σᵢⱼaᵢaⱼγ(sᵢ-sⱼ) ≤ 0. If the field is also wide stationary, γ(h) = C(0)-C(h) for every h ∈ ℝᵈ. The proof is choice-free.

Assuming AC, any index set T ⊆ ℝᵈ, mean m:T→ℝ, and real symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel K determine a unique probability measure on the cylinder sigma-algebra of ℝᵀ with the specified Gaussian finite-coordinate laws. The coordinate field has mean m and covariance K; no path continuity or joint measurability is asserted.

Assuming AC and DC, a real wide-stationary field on ℝᵈ with continuous covariance C has a unique finite positive Radon measure μ on the Pontryagin dual such that C(h) = ∫χ(h) μ(dχ), with total mass C(0). No density assertion is made.

seams_checked.note: The field definition extends finite-law shift invariance and finite-second-moment weak stationarity to admissible spatial translations. Reversing covariance arguments is harmless by real covariance symmetry. No time-series limit theorem is imported.

The discrete supplier uses the circle dual and angular frequencies. The spatial theorem independently invokes LCA Bochner on ℝᵈ with the same positive-character representation and AC/DC assumptions; it imports no density, angular normalization, or periodogram conclusion.

Spatial integration explicitly adds joint measurability. Lattice covariance reconciles its reversed argument order by symmetry, and the empirical semivariogram uses displacement-only increment second raw moments. The alias identity separately assumes an integrable spectral density.

The covariance formulation explicitly requires finite second moments. Its variogram remark retains the supplier's all-of-ℝᵈ domain and real zero-sum CND inequality and expressly does not infer augmented-system invertibility.
